Launchers know a server by the fingerprint of its TLS certificate. It's written to the log at every start: `TLS 1.3 enabled — certificate fingerprint (SHA-256): …`. The server passes it to NodeMP in every report, and a launcher accepts only that certificate, by address too. The fingerprint changes only if you lose or replace `node_cert.pem` and `node_key.pem`, so back them up. If the fingerprint changes, launchers that remembered the old one won't connect to a server that isn't listed ([Join by address](/players/join/#join-by-address)).

## Change or delete the key

On the **My servers** page, the **Rotate secret** button gives a new secret (also shown once), and the old one stops working. Put the new `host_secret` in and restart the server. Do this if the secret may have leaked. The **Delete** button deletes the key: the server keeps running but disappears from the list.

## The server isn't in the list

| In the log | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `The directory refused this server's credentials: …` | The Host ID or secret is wrong, the secret was rotated or the key was deleted. | Compare the key with the **My servers** page. If in doubt, rotate the secret and put in the new one. |
| `The directory refused this server: This server is banned from the directory.` | NodeMP's moderators blocked this server. | Ask the moderators on Discord. |
| `This server is NOT announced to a directory: …` | `url`, `host_id` or `host_secret` is missing. | Fill in all of them in `[listing]`. |
| `Refusing to announce this server: the [listing] url is plain http, …` | `url` has `http://`, and the secret would go in the clear. | Put in an address with `https://`. |
| `Could not reach the directory at https://api.nodemp.com: …` | There is no outgoing HTTPS, DNS doesn't work or NodeMP is unreachable. | On the server's machine, run `curl https://api.nodemp.com/healthz`. The server retries by itself. |
| `The directory answered 429 …` or `The directory answered 503 …` | Too many attempts in a short time (for example, the server restarts in a loop) or NodeMP is busy. NodeMP writes the reason after the colon. | Nothing: the server waits as long as NodeMP asks and tries again. |
| `not shown in the server browser: [listing] public is false; …` | `public = false` is set. | Remove it or set `public = true`, and restart the server. |
| `Not shown in the server browser: the directory's staff have hidden it` | NodeMP's moderators hid the server from the list. | Ask the moderators on Discord. |
| `Not shown in the server browser: it is banned from the directory` | NodeMP's moderators blocked this server. | Ask the moderators on Discord. |
| `Not shown in the server browser: another server key already announces this address and port, …` | Two keys announce the same address and port, and the list shows only one. | Delete the extra key on the **My servers** page. |
| `Listed in the server browser, but players cannot connect: …` | Players got join tickets, but none of them reached the server. | Forward the port from this line for TCP and UDP and open it in the firewall. |
| Players are refused with `The server could not verify your account with the directory (…)` | NodeMP was unreachable or overloaded when they joined. | Wait. On a server with Test Drive you can turn on `admit_when_down`. |

---

# Mods and maps

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/mods/

> How to add your own map, a car or another BeamNG mod to the server, how players get them and how to keep a mod from being sent.

Mods are ordinary BeamNG zip archives: a map, a car, a sound pack. The server hands them to players, and the launcher downloads them before the game starts. Players don't install mods by hand.

## Add a mod

1. Put the mod's zip into the `content/` folder next to `server.toml`. In Docker that's `data/content/`.
2. Restart the server. It reads the folder only at start.

The log then has a line such as `serving 2 mods (148.3 MB) from content/`. If a file isn't a zip, the server skips it and writes `'…' is not a ZIP file and will be ignored`.

After replacing or deleting a zip, restart the server too.

## A map of your own

Put the map's zip into `content/` and set the map in `[server] map`:

```toml
[server]
map = "/levels/my_map/info.json"
```

Here `my_map` is the name of the map's folder inside the archive, under `levels/`. To find it, open the archive and look at which folder is in `levels/`.

If the map has a picture of its own, the server shows it in the server list ([The picture](/hosting/registering/#the-picture)).

## How players get mods

Before joining, the launcher downloads from the server the archives the player doesn't have yet and keeps them in a cache ([Join a server](/players/join/#look-at-a-server)). Every new player waits for every megabyte to download, and the **Download size** filter in the list hides heavy servers, so remove the mods you don't need.

At most `[network] max_concurrent_downloads` players download mods from the server at once, and `download_rate_mb` and `download_total_rate_mb` cap the per-player and total speed ([Settings reference](/hosting/configuration/#network)). To offload the server's link, upload the same zip archives to a web server or CDN and set the base URL in `[server] mods_url`. If a file fails to download from that URL, the launcher fetches it from the server.

## A mod that isn't sent

Some mods may not be redistributed, and players have to download them themselves. Open `content/mods.json` (the server writes it) and set `"protected": true` for such an archive:

```json
"big-map.zip": { "protected": true }
```

The entry has other fields too; leave them alone and change only `protected`. The server then no longer sends that file. The launcher of a player who doesn't have the mod explains which cache folder to put it in. The mark stays even if you replace the archive.

## Plugins' client scripts

Plugins can also send Lua scripts to players, but that is a different mechanism: the scripts arrive on join, and you don't put them in `content/` ([Plugins on the server](/hosting/resources/)).

The two mechanisms work together too: a plugin's scripts can switch on Lua from a mod in `content/`. The mod then needs no start script of its own (`scripts/…/modScript.lua`): the plugin loads its Lua and switches it off when the player leaves. How to do it: [Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/).

---

# Plugins on the server

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/resources/

> How to install a plugin on the server, configure, reload and obfuscate it, and what native modules are.

A plugin is a folder in `resources/` with Lua code that runs on the server and, if needed, scripts that the server sends to players. Chat commands, rules, game modes and admin tools are all plugins. How to write them: [Plugin development](/plugins/overview/).

## Install a plugin

1. Copy the plugin's whole folder into `resources/` next to `server.toml`. If there is no `resources/` folder yet, create it. In Docker that's `data/resources/`.
2. Restart the server.

The server logs every plugin it loads:

```text
demo-numbers v1.0 loaded — lua · server 1 file · 1 client file
1 resource · 1 module loaded
```

Chat works without plugins; chat commands such as `/pm` come from plugins.

The server archive has an `examples/` folder next to the program with ready-made plugins. To try an example, copy its folder into `resources/`. The copy is yours: you can change it, and updating the server won't touch it. Which examples there are: [The example plugins](/plugins/examples/).

## A plugin's settings

A plugin's folder can hold a `resource.toml` file. What a host needs in it is the `[config]` table with the plugin's own settings. The plugin's author says which keys it takes. For example, for `vehicle-cleanup`:

```toml
[config]
deleteIdleAfterSeconds = 600
maxWorldVehicles = 20
```

After an edit, restart the server or reload the plugin.

## Reload a plugin

The `reload <name>` command in the server console starts a plugin's server part again without restarting the whole server. The server packs the client scripts once, at start, so changes to them reach players only after a restart.

## Obfuscating client scripts

Before sending the scripts a plugin gives to players, the server scrambles them (`[resources] obfuscate`, on by default) to make them harder to copy. Prometheus, a Lua program in the `tools/` folder, does this, and it needs Lua 5.1. It's already in the Windows archive and in the Docker image; on Linux you install it separately ([Install Lua 5.1](/hosting/linux/#install-lua-51)).

When all is well, the log has `client obfuscation ready · runner … · Prometheus (cache .obfcache)`. If not, the server still works and sends the scripts as they are, and the log explains what is missing. To check the setup, run `Node-Server --obf-selftest`: on success it prints `[obf-selftest] available=1`.

The plugin chooses how hard to scramble with the `[client] obfuscation` key in `resource.toml`: `none`, `light` (the default), `medium` or `strong`. The results are cached in `.obfcache/`, and you can delete that folder at any time.

The server also checks the syntax of client scripts while packing them. It still sends a script with an error, but warns in the log: `… client file 'main.lua' has a syntax error: …`.

## Native modules

A native module is a compiled library (`.dll` or `.so`) in the `modules/` folder next to the program. Modules load before plugins. The archive already has the database module for plugins ([The db module](/plugins/database/)).

At load the server checks which interface version a module was built for. It doesn't load an incompatible module and asks for a rebuild. How to add a module in Docker: [Plugins and mods](/hosting/docker/#plugins-and-mods).

---

# Console, kicks and bans

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/administration/

> The server console's commands, how to kick and ban a player, lift a ban, restart the server with a warning and what to look for in the log.

## The console

A server started in a terminal takes commands right in its window. On Windows that is the `Node-Server.exe` window, on Linux the terminal you started it from.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `help` | The list of commands. |
| `status` | Version, uptime, players, cars, plugins, memory. |
| `players` | Everyone on the server: id, name, ping, cars and address (the last part is hidden). |
| `kick <id\|name> [reason]` | Disconnect a player and show them the reason. Put a name with spaces in quotes. |
| `say <text>` | A system message in the chat for all players. |
| `reload <resource>` | Restart a plugin. |
| `stop` | Stop the server. `exit` and `quit` do the same. |

Plugins can add commands of their own, and `help` lists them under `from resources:` with the name of the plugin. Input that no command takes gets the answer `unknown command, try help`.

A player kicked without a reason sees `Kicked by the server`. Players have no access to the console: a `/kick 1` typed in chat stays a chat line until some plugin takes it.

A systemd service has no console ([A systemd service](/hosting/linux/#a-systemd-service)). In Docker the console appears if you give the container a terminal ([The console](/hosting/docker/#the-console)).

### The chat in the console

The console shows the chat as players write, with the player's id:

```text
17:51:12.345  Chat   › (0) Alice: hello
17:51:16.000  Chat   › System -> all: Restart in 5 minutes  [console]
```

If a line wasn't sent, the reason is written beside it, and a line that a plugin took as a command is marked `[handled by a resource]`. The arguments of commands with passwords (`/login`, `/register` and the others in `[chat] masked_commands`) are replaced with `***`. `[chat] log = false` takes the chat out of the console and the log.

## Kicks and bans

You can kick from the console with the command above. There is no ban command in the console: plugins ban, for example with a `/ban` command for moderators ([example](/plugins/chat/)).

### Bans

Bans are kept in `bans.json` in the working directory, as one JSON object. A record's key names what is blocked: an address, a NodeMP account as `nodemp:<id>`, or a launcher installation as `install:<id>` (64 hexadecimal digits). The value holds the reason, the time and the player's name:

```json
{
  "203.0.113.7": { "reason": "Spam", "at": 1789558100, "name": "Bob" },
  "nodemp:108": { "reason": "Spam", "at": 1789558100, "name": "Bob" },
  "install:6b46e2582a74234a47a4fa2c7046023be8ea6043e62ff00f1d6c166d39f57fd4": { "reason": "Spam", "at": 1789558100, "name": "Bob" }
}
```

A timed ban also has the field `"until"`: the end time in Unix seconds. When it comes, the server removes the ban by itself.

Banning a player who is on the server blocks their address and, if they are signed in, their account, so the ban works from another network too. On a listed server it also blocks the player's launcher installation, whose id the server gets from NodeMP when the player joins: that launcher can't join with any account or in Test Drive. The installation id is different on each server (other servers know the same launcher by other ids) and changes when NodeMP changes its key, after which a ban on the old id no longer matches. A banned player sees the reason when joining, or `You are banned from this server` if there is none.

NodeMP can ban an account on every server at once. Such a player gets no join ticket for any listed server, and a player who is already playing is disconnected at the server's next report to NodeMP, with `This account is banned from NodeMP`.

To lift a ban, stop the server and run:

```text
Node-Server --bans list
Node-Server --bans remove 203.0.113.7
Node-Server --bans remove nodemp:108
Node-Server --bans remove install:6b46e2582a74234a47a4fa2c7046023be8ea6043e62ff00f1d6c166d39f57fd4
```

`list` shows all bans, and `remove` lifts one: by address, by `nodemp:<id>` or the bare account number, or by `install:<id>`. You can also edit the file by hand, but only while the server is stopped. A running server keeps the list in memory and rewrites the file at the next ban.

## Restarting with a warning

`stop` disconnects everyone at once. To warn players first, a plugin schedules the restart: the call `node.server.shutdown("Nightly restart", 5 * 60 * 1000)` stops the server in five minutes. Players see that reason, plugins save their data and the server exits with code 0. A systemd service with `Restart=always` or a container with `restart: unless-stopped` then starts it again. An example with a countdown in chat: [Timers and coroutines](/plugins/concurrency/).

## The log

Everything the server writes to the console also goes to `logs/server.log`, and the file has more. The console shows what needs a reaction: joins and leaves, spawns, refusals, chat, warnings and errors. Statistics and housekeeping lines, such as `netstats`, go only to the file unless `[logs] details = true`. The server starts a new file at every start and when the current one grows past 50 MB, and keeps five old ones as `server.1.log`, `server.2.log` and so on (`[logs] max_size_mb` and `keep`).

The main lines of the log:

| Line | What it means |
|---|---|
| `server is ready` | The server has fully started. |
| `started, but … failed — what they do may not work` | Some part didn't start ([The server won't start](/hosting/troubleshooting/#the-server-wont-start)). |
| `listed in the server browser` | The server is in the list ([Get listed](/hosting/registering/)). |
| `<name> kicked — <reason>` | The server refused a player or ended their session, in the same words the player saw. |
| `netstats id=… rtt=… loss=…` | In the file, every 15 seconds for each player: ping, traffic, loss ([A player says it lags](/hosting/troubleshooting/#a-player-says-it-lags)). |

## A player can't get in

The player usually sends the text from the launcher. What it means is in [Error messages](/reference/error-codes/), and in the log the same text is in a line with the `Kick` tag. If several players from one place can't get in, read [Players are refused at the door](/hosting/troubleshooting/#players-are-refused-at-the-door).

---

# The join queue

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/join-queue/

> How a full server lets players with an account wait for a place, the limits of the queue, what the console shows and how plugins steer the queue.

When the server is full, a player with an account doesn't have to try again and again: the player waits in the server's queue, and the launcher gets everything ready meanwhile. The queue is on by default on every listed server. `[queue]` sets it up ([Settings reference](/hosting/configuration/#queue)), and `enabled = false` turns it off.

## Who waits

- Only players with an account. A full server answers a guest in Test Drive with `Server full!`, and the one-time join ticket isn't spent.
- Only players whose launcher can wait. A launcher that can't gets `Server full!` too.
- Banned players are refused, not queued.
- A player who restores a broken session within `[network] disconnect_sec` skips the queue, and so does a player a plugin holds a place for (`playerConnectRequest` answers `true`): both are let in over `max_players`.

## How a waiting player gets in

While a player waits, the server checks their game files and sends the mod list, and the launcher downloads what is missing: `downloads_while_waiting` players at once, in queue order. The downloads of players joining a free place count too and go first, so the queue doesn't slow a join down. A waiting player can download only the files in the mod list, each once.

A free place goes to the first player in the queue whose mods are ready. The first in line keeps their place while downloading, but a ready player behind them gets in earlier. Then the game starts and the player joins like any other, with no second file check and no second download.

Once a player has a place, the queue no longer hurries them. The usual limits remain: a download that makes no progress for `[network] download_stall_sec` seconds is cut off.

A waiting launcher pings the server every 30 seconds, and a waiting connection that stays silent for 90 seconds loses its place. The server sends a place in the queue only when it changes, and no more often than once every 5 seconds.

## Limits

- At most `max_waiting` players wait in total (50). The next one is refused with `The server is full and so is its join queue`.
- At most `max_waiting_per_ip` players wait from one address (1). Addresses in `[network] connection_limit_exempt`, such as a local network, aren't limited. A second player from the same address is refused with `Someone from your address is already in this server's join queue`.
- One place per account. Joining from another launcher takes over the place, and the old connection is closed.
- Whoever leaves loses the place. If a player clicked **Cancel**, closed the launcher or was removed from the queue, the launcher fetches a new join ticket by itself at the next attempt, and the player goes to the end.
- No-shows. A player who got a place and left without reaching the world `max_no_shows` times (3) within `no_show_window_min` minutes (60) can't join this server's queue for `no_show_bar_min` minutes (30). The player is told until when. A kick, a ban or a server stop isn't a no-show, and joining while a place is free still works.

A waiting player costs the server about 135 KB of memory and no thread of their own: 50 waiting players take about 7 MB. A waiting player doesn't take one of the `max_connections` slots for incoming connections either.

## What the player sees

The launcher shows the place in the queue in its join line ([When the server is full](/players/join/#when-the-server-is-full)). The texts of the refusals and how the launcher shows them: [The server's refusals and kicks](/reference/error-codes/#the-servers-refusals-and-kicks).

## What the console shows

```text
20:41:07.112  Join   › Kayla waits in the join queue (3 of 7)
20:47:59.430  Join   › Kayla gets a place after 412 s in the join queue; 6 waiting
20:48:12.015  Leave  › Ivan left the join queue at 4 after 95 s (Connection closed by the client); 5 waiting
20:48:30.201  Kick   › 203.0.113.7 refused at the join queue: The server is full and so is its join queue
20:52:44.876  Leave  › Ivan (account 1042) left without entering the world after its turn in the join queue: 2 of 3 within 60 min
21:19:03.548  Join   › Kayla has been joining for 31 min, longer than joins here usually take (15 min); its game attached and is loading
```

The last line reports a slow join: one that takes four times as long as the median of the recent joins to this server, and at least 15 minutes. The server doesn't interrupt such a join, and plugins get the `playerJoinSlow` event.

## For plugins

Every function is described under [`node.queue`](/plugins/api/lua/#nodequeue--the-join-queue), and every event in the [event reference](/plugins/api/events/). A player in the queue has no player id yet, so the queue names the player by account id.

- `queueJoinRequest` asks whether a player may wait, and where. Return `false` and a reason to refuse, or a position to put the player there.
- `queueAdmitRequest` asks who gets a free place. The candidates are the ready players. Return an account id to choose, or `false` to leave the place free for now.
- `queueAdmitted`, `queueLeft` and `queueNoShow` say what became of a waiting player, and `playerJoinSlow` reports a slow join.

League members wait at the front:

<!-- doctest: skip needs a full server with players waiting in its queue -->
```lua
local members = { [1042] = true, [2077] = true }

local function put_members_first(request)
    if members[request.accountId] then return { position = 1 } end
end

node.on("queueJoinRequest", put_members_first)
```

During a race the queue lets nobody in, and waiting players read the note under their place:

<!-- doctest: skip needs a full server with players waiting in its queue -->
```lua
node.queue.pause("The race ends at 21:30, places open after it")
-- ...
node.queue.resume()
```

`node.queue.list()` returns the waiting players in order, `move` and `first` change a place, `remove` removes a player with a reason, `admit` lets a player in over `max_players` as soon as their mods are ready, and `limits` and `setLimits` read and change the `[queue]` numbers until the server restarts.

<!-- doctest: skip needs a full server with players waiting in its queue -->
```lua
for _, waiter in ipairs(node.queue.list()) do
    node.log(string.format("%d. %s%s", waiter.position, waiter.name, waiter.ready and " (ready)" or ""))
end
node.queue.setLimits({ maxWaiting = 20 })
```

---

# Strict file check

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/strict-verification/

> What verify = "strict" checks, how to make the reference manifest, where to put it and what to do after a game update.

`[integrity] verify = "strict"` is the strictest check of the game files. The other levels compare the player's install with the list of files that comes with the game, and a player can edit that list together with the files. The strict check compares the install with a reference manifest: a description of a clean install that you make once per game version.

It's for races and tournaments where everyone must have the same game. For freeroam the default check, `size`, is usually enough.

## What it checks

The player's launcher runs the check and the server judges the result. A player passes when everything listed here matches.

- The files in the manifest. The size of each is compared. The game's code (`lua/`, `ui/`), everything in `Bin64/` and `BinLinux/` and every `.exe` in the game folder are also compared by SHA-256, so an edit that keeps the size is visible too.
- The game's archives. The table of contents of each `.zip` is compared: the name, size and CRC-32 of every file inside.
- The whole game folder. An extra file is an error, except logs, caches and what the game and Windows write themselves. An extra `.dll` in `Bin64/` is always an error.
- The game's user folder (`…\BeamNG.drive\current`). What the game and the player write is allowed there: settings, screenshots, replays, saves, caches and temporary files, logs, mods in `mods/`, work from the built-in editors, your own car configurations (`vehicles/<model>/<name>.pc` with a picture). Everything else in `vehicles/`, `levels/`, `lua/`, `ui/`, `art/`, `scripts/`, `gameplay/` and in folders named like the game's folders counts as a substitution.

## What it doesn't catch

The strict check keeps honest players on a clean game, but it doesn't protect against cheating.

- Inside the archives only the table of contents is compared. CRC-32 can be forged by someone who edits an archive on purpose.
- The launcher runs on the player's computer, and the player controls the computer.
- Files other than code and programs are compared by size only.
- The manifest is only as clean as the install it was made from.

So you still need rules on the server side, in your plugins.

## Make the manifest

The generator is built into the server. Run it on a computer with Windows and a clean BeamNG.drive of the same version your players have: verify the game files in Steam and remove third-party programs and mods from the game folder. You need the Windows build of the server:

```powershell
$game = "C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\BeamNG.drive"
.\Node-Server.exe --gen-integrity $game
```

The argument is the game's main folder, the one that holds `integrity.json`. A Linux or Docker server has no game, so make the manifest where the game is installed and copy it to the server.

You can set the file name and the game version by hand: `--out FILE` names the file, and `--game-version V` gives the version instead of the one recorded in `integrity.json`.

At the end the generator prints a summary, including a `hash` line that names the manifest, and the path of the file, for example `integrity\<game version>.manifest`. Two runs on the same install give the same file. If something goes wrong, no file is written and the generator says `integrity manifest NOT written: …`.

## Put the manifest on the server

By default (`[integrity] auto_fetch = true`), if `verify = "strict"` is set and `integrity/` has no `.manifest` file, the server downloads the official reference manifest from NodeMP (`[integrity] url` and `game_version`) at startup and saves it in `integrity/`. Generating one by hand with `--gen-integrity` is only needed when `auto_fetch` is off or for a custom game build.

1. Copy the file into `integrity/` in the server's working directory. In Docker that's `data/integrity/`.
2. Set `verify = "strict"` in `[integrity]` (in Docker, the variable `NODE_VERIFY_GAME=strict`).
3. Restart the server.

The log then has `strict game verification ON: reference manifest for game … (…)`.

The folder must hold exactly one manifest. The launcher doesn't tell the server which game version it has, so with two files the server can't choose and lets nobody in. With no file it lets nobody in either and asks the host to make a manifest.

The manifest is also loaded on a server with another check level. A plugin can then start a strict check itself when it needs one, and refuse nobody at the door.

## After a game update

A manifest describes one game version. When BeamNG updates, the server stops letting in players who have the new version. Make a new manifest from the updated clean install, replace the old file (there is still one file) and restart the server. Launchers notice the new manifest and download it at their next join. Now players who haven't updated the game yet are refused, and updating in Steam fixes that.

## What the player sees

A clean install joins as usual. What the launcher shows on a mismatch and what the player does: [When something breaks](/players/troubleshooting/#a-strict-server-refuses-you).

During play the launcher checks again when files change, and the server asks for a check every `[integrity] recheck_sec` seconds, by default every ten minutes ([Settings reference](/hosting/configuration/#integrity)). If a mismatch is found, the session ends. Checks during a session don't recompute the game's programs: a replaced library takes effect only after the game restarts, and the next join checks the programs again.

## For plugin authors

`player:verify(level)` asks the player's launcher to check the files right now, and the `playerVerifyReported` event arrives with every check result. On a server with `verify = "off"` that is the only consequence, and this is how you build a check that doesn't kick anyone out. Details: [Lua API reference](/plugins/api/lua/) and [events](/plugins/api/events/).

---

# Updating the server

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/updating/

> How to check the server's version, install a new release on Windows, Linux and in Docker, what survives an update and when players need a new launcher.

An update replaces the program and the folders that come with it (`tools/`, `modules/`, `examples/`), or the Docker image. Your data stays ([What survives an update](#what-survives-an-update)).

## Which version is running

```bash
./Node-Server --version
```

The command prints `Node-Server v` and the version number. The startup banner shows the same version.

## Where releases are

The archives are on the [download page](https://nodemp.com/download) in the **Your own server** block. Every server release is also on [GitHub](https://github.com/NodeMP-BeamNG/releases/releases) under a tag `server-v<version>`. The release description says what changed, whether any defaults changed and whether the protocol version changed. Read it before you update.

## Windows

1. Stop the server.
2. Download the new archive and unpack it into the same folder over the old files. When Explorer asks about files with the same names, choose to replace them.
3. Start the server and check the version in the banner.

To unpack over the old files from PowerShell:

```powershell
$zip = "$HOME\Downloads\Node-Server-<version>-windows-x64.zip"
Expand-Archive $zip -DestinationPath C:\NodeMP -Force
```

Without `-Force` the command refuses to overwrite files.

## Linux

With the service from [Server on Linux](/hosting/linux/#a-systemd-service):

```bash
cd /tmp
version=<version>
url=https://github.com/NodeMP-BeamNG/releases/releases/download/server-v$version
curl -LO "$url/Node-Server-$version-linux-x64.tar.gz"
curl -LO "$url/Node-Server-$version-linux-x64.tar.gz.sha256"
sha256sum -c Node-Server-$version-linux-x64.tar.gz.sha256
```

Then stop the service, unpack the archive over the old files and start it again:

```bash
sudo systemctl stop nodemp
sudo tar -xzf Node-Server-$version-linux-x64.tar.gz -C /opt/nodemp
sudo chown -R nodemp:nodemp /opt/nodemp
sudo systemctl start nodemp
```

Unpacking over the folder replaces exactly what the archive holds. The `resources/` folder, including the examples you copied into it, isn't in the archive, and unpacking doesn't touch it.

## Docker

Pull the new image:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/nodemp-beamng/server:<tag>
```

In `compose.yaml`, change the `image:` line to the new tag and run `docker compose up -d`. With `docker run`, remove the old container and start a new one with the same `-v` and the same variables. The `data/` folder doesn't change. To roll back, put the previous tag back.

## What survives an update

- `server.toml` stays as it is. A new setting that is neither in the file nor in the environment takes its default.
- `node_cert.pem` and `node_key.pem` aren't in the archive and are created only if they are missing. Don't lose them ([The server's fingerprint](/hosting/registering/#the-servers-fingerprint)).
- `resources/`, `content/`, `storage/` and `bans.json` are yours, and an update doesn't touch them. If your plugin uses the database module's `db.lua`, copy the new `modules/db.lua` into it.
- `integrity/` belongs to a game version, not a server version. After a BeamNG update, make the manifest again ([Strict file check](/hosting/strict-verification/#after-a-game-update)).
- The server doesn't load a native module built for an incompatible interface version ([Native modules](/hosting/resources/#native-modules)). Lua plugins don't need rebuilding.

## When players need a new launcher

The network protocol between the launcher and the server has a version number, and it must be the same on both ([Wire protocol](/reference/protocol/#versions)). If a release changes the protocol, its description says so prominently, and a launcher that is behind is refused and offers **Update now**. The launcher updates the client mod by itself before every join. Update the server when players get the new launcher: with a launcher newer than the server, players are refused with a message that explains the server is behind ([Error messages](/reference/error-codes/#the-servers-refusals-and-kicks)).

---

# When the server misbehaves

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/hosting/troubleshooting/

> The server won't start, can't be reached, refuses players at the door, Docker surprises, a player says it lags. What the log says and what to do.

Everything the server can tell you, it writes to the console and to `logs/server.log`. Start with the log.

## The server won't start

When the server can't start, it explains why, prints `Closing in 10 seconds` and exits with code 1. A systemd service sees that as a failure, not a normal stop.

| Message | What happened | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `Cannot listen on port … (…): the port is already in use (…). …` | The port is taken. Most often it's a second copy of the server that nobody stopped. | Stop the other copy or set another port. |
| `Cannot listen on port … (…): … failed: …. Closing.` | The port couldn't be opened for another reason; the system's own words are in the line. | Read them. Check that `[server] address` is an address of this machine. |
| `[server] address = "…" is not an IP address (…); the server cannot listen. …` | `address` (or `NODE_IP`) isn't an address. | Set it back to `"::"`. |
| `Error parsing config file value: …: the table […] appears twice. …` | A table is written twice in `server.toml`, usually a second `[listing]`. | Move the keys into the first table and delete the second. |
| `Error parsing config file value: …: the key … is given twice. …` | One setting is written twice in one table. | Delete one of the lines. |
| `Error parsing config file value: …: … -- the line reads …` | Another mistake in the file; the line is quoted. | Fix the line, or delete `server.toml` so that the server writes a new one. |
| `[network] timers must satisfy lag_grace_sec < seat_takeover_sec <= seat_release_sec <= disconnect_sec …` | The `[network]` timers are out of order. | Fix them in `server.toml` or in the `NODE_NETWORK_*` variables. |
| `TLS: cannot write … (…); the certificate pair is generated on the first start, …` | The server can't write the certificate where the settings point. | Point `[network] tls_cert` and `tls_key` at files in a folder you can write to. In Docker, see [below](#docker). |

If the server started but some part of it didn't, the log has `started, but … failed — what they do may not work`, and the lines above it say why. The server keeps running.

## The server can't be reached

The launcher says it can't reach the server, or the list marks the server as one players can't connect to.

1. Open the port for both TCP and UDP. TCP is for joining and everything reliable, UDP for the cars' positions. Check the firewall on the machine and the port forwarding on the router.
2. Test from outside: a connection from your own network says nothing about the router. Ask a friend or use a port-checking service.
3. Leave `[server] address` at `"::"`. The server then listens on every address, and the log confirms it: `listening on [::]:30814 (tcp, tls 1.3, dual-stack: IPv4 + IPv6)`.
4. In Docker, publish the port the server listens on: `-p 30814:30814/tcp` and `-p 30814:30814/udp`, or the one set in `NODE_PORT` ([Server in Docker](/hosting/docker/#run-it)).

Players on the same network as the server join by its local address, such as `192.168.1.20:30814`.

## Players are refused at the door

A player says the launcher showed `TLS handshake failed: unexpected eof while reading`. Often it's several players from one place, or everyone from one VPN. The server limits how many connections from one address may be joining at the same time and closes the extra ones before the handshake. The server's log shows this under the `Net` tag.

- The limit is `[network] max_connections_per_ip`, 32 by default. Raise it if many players come from one address: a club, a carrier's NAT, a VPN exit.
- `[network] connection_limit_exempt` lists address ranges without the per-address limit. By default these are local and private networks, which covers a VPN or proxy on the same machine as the server.
- The launchers' background polls of the server list count as connections too.

Every connection that fails before joining is written to the log under the `Net` tag with the address and the reason: a timeout, not TLS 1.3, not TLS at all, the client closed the connection.

## Docker

### The server stops right after starting

The log has `TLS: cannot write /opt/node/node_key.pem (…)`. Inside the image the program's folder is read-only, and the certificate is written there by default. Move it to the data folder:

```bash
-e NODE_TLS_CERT=/data/tls/node_cert.pem
-e NODE_TLS_KEY=/data/tls/node_key.pem
```

The image creates `/data/tls` at every start. Why you must not lose these files: [The server's fingerprint](/hosting/registering/#the-servers-fingerprint).

### `server.toml` isn't read

This is by design: the image sets `NODE_PROVIDER_DISABLE_CONFIG=true`, and every setting comes from the `NODE_*` variables. To make the server read and write `/data/server.toml`, set `NODE_PROVIDER_DISABLE_CONFIG=false`.

### Permission denied at start

The server runs as user 10001 and can't write to the data folder or read the files you copied into it. Run `sudo chown -R 10001:10001 data` and restart the container.

### The console doesn't respond

A container without a terminal has no console ([The console](/hosting/docker/#the-console)).

## The server isn't listed

The log says why: [Get listed](/hosting/registering/#the-server-isnt-in-the-list). A closed port doesn't remove the server from the list: the list marks it as one players can't connect to ([above](#the-server-cant-be-reached)).

## A player says it lags

Find the player's `netstats` lines in `logs/server.log`, one every 15 seconds. `rtt` is the round trip in milliseconds, `loss` the share of lost UDP packets. If the numbers are high for one player and fine for the others, it's their connection: send them [A bad connection and VPNs](/players/connection/). If it's bad for everyone, the problem is the server's own connection.

---

# Overview

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/plugins/overview/

> What NodeMP plugins can do, the kinds of plugin, how the server and client halves work, and what to read first.

A plugin changes how the server behaves: chat commands, rules, game modes, admin tools, a link to a website or Discord. The server itself passes data between players and keeps order; plugins make one server differ from another.

## What you can do

- React to events: a player joined, spawned a car, got into it, wrote in chat.
- Refuse actions: keep a player out, forbid cars, edits and paint jobs, filter chat.
- Manage players and cars: kick and ban, seat a player in a car, teleport, freeze, put tags and locks on cars.
- Keep data across restarts, work with a database and call web services over HTTP.
- Send players your own Lua code to run in the game, and exchange messages with it.

## Kinds of plugin

| Kind | What it is | When to choose it |
|---|---|---|
| Lua plugin | A folder in `resources/` with Lua 5.4 code. Lua is built into the server. | Almost always: rules, commands, modes, anything about the game. |
| JavaScript plugin | The same folder with JavaScript code. Needs the `js-host` module ([JavaScript plugins](/plugins/js-host/)). | When you need an npm package or prefer JavaScript. |
| Native module | A C or C++ library in `modules/` ([Native modules](/plugins/native-modules/)). | When code runs for every packet or frame and Lua can't keep up. |

## The server half and the client half

A plugin can have two halves:

- The server half (`server/main.lua`) runs on the server. It has the `node` API: players, cars, events, timers, storage, HTTP.
- The client half (files in `client/`) runs in the game of every player. It has everything a game mod has, plus NodeMP functions for talking to the server ([Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/)).

The halves talk through wire events: the client sends `node.emitServer("name", data)`, the server receives it in `node.on("name", handler)` and answers with `player:send` or `node.broadcast`.

The handlers of all plugins run one after another on a single thread, so a slow handler holds up the rest ([Timers and coroutines](/plugins/concurrency/)). Plugins talk to each other over the [bus](/plugins/bus/).

## Where to start

1. [Your first plugin](/plugins/getting-started/): from an empty folder to a chat command and a client half.
2. [How a plugin is built](/plugins/resources/): files, `resource.toml`, reloading, load errors.
3. The topics, in order: [Events](/plugins/events/), [Players and vehicles](/plugins/players-and-vehicles/), [Chat and commands](/plugins/chat/), [Timers and coroutines](/plugins/concurrency/), [Storage and files](/plugins/storage/), [The db module](/plugins/database/), [HTTP requests](/plugins/http/), [The bus between plugins](/plugins/bus/), [Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/), [API conventions](/plugins/conventions/).
4. [The example plugins](/plugins/examples/): ready-made plugins from the server archive.
5. [Moving from other platforms](/plugins/migrating/): if you have written plugins for another multiplayer mod.

Keep the [API reference](/plugins/api/lua/) at hand: it lists every function and every [event](/plugins/api/events/). It is generated from the API description.

---

# Your first plugin

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/plugins/getting-started/

> Build a plugin from an empty folder, step by step. It greets players, answers a chat command, reads its settings, runs a client half and reloads.

These steps build `greeter`, a plugin that greets players, answers `/online`, takes its greeting from the settings and shows a message in the player's game. There is nothing to install: Lua is built into the server.

You need a server ([Run a server](/hosting/quick-start/)) and the launcher to join it.

## 1. The folder

Plugins live in `resources/`, next to `server.toml`. Make this tree:

```text
resources/
└── greeter/
    ├── resource.toml
    └── server/
        └── main.lua
```

The folder name becomes the plugin's name unless `resource.toml` says otherwise. The `client/` folder comes in step 7.

## 2. resource.toml

```toml
name = "greeter"
version = "1.0"
```

That is enough for now. Every key of the file is on [How a plugin is built](/plugins/resources/#resourcetoml).

## 3. The server half

`server/main.lua` runs once, when the server loads the plugin. Top-level code subscribes to events; the server calls the handlers later, when something happens.

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
node.log("greeter loaded")

local function greet(player)
    node.log("%s joined", player.name)
    player:tell("Welcome, %s!", player.name)
end

node.on("playerJoined", greet)

local function sayGoodbye(player, reason)
    node.log("%s left: %s", player.name, reason)
end

node.on("playerLeft", sayGoodbye)

-- expect: greeter loaded
-- expect: Alice joined
-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*Welcome, Alice!
-- expect: Alice left: \S
```

- `node.log` writes to the server console under the plugin's name. Extra arguments work as in `string.format`.
- `node.on(name, handler)` subscribes a function to an event. `playerJoined` passes a `Player` object: `name` and `id` are fields, `tell` and `kick` are methods.
- `player:tell` writes a system line into that player's chat. Chat is built into the server, so no other plugin is needed.
- `playerLeft` also gets the reason the session ended.

## 4. Start the server

Start the server. The console shows your line, then the server's line about the plugin:

```text
greeter · greeter loaded
greeter v1.0 loaded — lua · server 1 file · 0 client files
```

Join the server. The console shows `greeter · <your name> joined` and the chat shows the greeting.

## 5. A chat command

Commands are ordinary chat lines starting with `/`. Every line passes through `chatMessageRequest` before the server sends it on. A handler that recognizes its command returns `{ handled = true }`: nobody sees the line, and the plugin sends its own reply.

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "/online"}]]} -->
```lua
local function answerOnline(player, msg)
    if msg.text ~= "/online" then return end
    local names = {}
    for _, p in ipairs(node.players.all()) do
        names[#names + 1] = p.name
    end
    player:tell("Online (%d): %s", #names, table.concat(names, ", "))
    return { handled = true }
end

node.on("chatMessageRequest", answerOnline)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*Online \(1\): Alice
```

For any other line the handler returns nothing (a bare `return`), so the line goes to chat as usual. More on commands: [Chat and commands](/plugins/chat/).

## 6. Settings

Settings the host can change go in the `[config]` table of `resource.toml`:

```toml
[config]
greeting = "Hello from the docs"
```

The plugin reads them as `node.config`:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"config": {"greeting": "Hello from the docs"}} -->
```lua
local greeting = node.config.greeting or "Welcome"

local function greetFromConfig(player)
    player:tell("%s, %s!", greeting, player.name)
end

node.on("playerJoined", greetFromConfig)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*Hello from the docs, Alice!
```

`node.config` is read once, when the plugin loads. After editing the file, reload the plugin ([below](#8-reload-the-plugin)).

## 7. The client half

Files in `client/` run in the game of every player ([Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/)). Let the server send the player an event when they join:

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local function sendHello(player)
    player:send("greeter:hello", { text = "Welcome, " .. player.name })
end

node.on("playerJoined", sendHello)

-- expect-client: Alice greeter:hello .*Welcome, Alice
```

`player:send(name, data)` sends a wire event to that player, and a table becomes JSON. Create `client/main.lua`: it catches the event, shows the text on screen and answers the server.

<!-- doctest: client -->
```lua
local function showHello(data)
    local hello = jsonDecode(data)
    ui_message(hello.text, 8, "greeter")
    node.emitServer("greeter:seen", hello.text)
end

node.on("greeter:hello", showHello)
```

On the client a handler gets the data as the string the server sent, so the game's `jsonDecode` parses it. `ui_message` is the game's function for an on-screen message. `node.emitServer` sends a wire event back, again as a string. The server half receives it:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["greeter:seen", "Welcome, Alice"]]} -->
```lua
local function logSeen(player, text)
    node.log("%s saw: %s", player.name, text)
end

node.on("greeter:seen", logSeen)

-- expect: Alice saw: Welcome, Alice
```

Name wire events `<plugin>:<what>`, in lowercase ([Events](/plugins/events/#kinds-of-events)).

## 8. Reload the plugin

A changed server half needs no server restart. Type in the server console:

```text
reload greeter
```

The plugin loads again from its folder. Changes in `client/` reach players only after a server restart ([How a plugin is built](/plugins/resources/#reloading)).

## 9. When something breaks

An error in a handler stops neither the server nor the plugin. The server logs it with the file, line and traceback, and calls the handler again on the next event.

```text
greeter · error in builtin 'playerJoined': …/server/main.lua:4: attempt to …
```

How this line looks for timers, coroutines and load errors: [API conventions](/plugins/conventions/#errors-in-handlers).

---

# How a plugin is built

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/plugins/resources/

> The files of a plugin, every key of resource.toml, the Lua environment, code in several files, reloading, load errors and the log.

A plugin is a folder inside `resources/`. The server loads every such folder when it starts.

## The files

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `resource.toml` | The plugin's description. Optional: without it the folder name is the plugin's name and the rest takes the defaults below. |
| `server/main.lua` | Entry point of the server half. |
| `server/*.lua` | The rest of the server code, loaded with `require` ([below](#several-files)). |
| `client/**/*.lua` | The client half ([Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/)). |
| `client/lua/vehicle/*.lua` | Client files that run inside the player's cars ([Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/#files-that-run-inside-the-car)). |
| anything else | Your data: read and write it with `node.fs`. |

The server skips a folder that has neither a server entry point nor client files.

## resource.toml

```toml
name = "race"
version = "1.2"

[server]
main = "server/main.lua"

[client]
files = ["main.lua", "ui.lua"]
obfuscation = "medium"

[config]
laps = 3
```

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | the folder name | The plugin's name in the log, in the `reload` command and in bus messages. |
| `version` | none | Shown in the log next to the name. |
| `type` | `"lua"` | What runs the server half. `"js"` needs the `js-host` module ([JavaScript plugins](/plugins/js-host/)). |
| `[server] main` | `"server/main.lua"` | The entry point, a path from the plugin's folder. |
| `[client] files` | every `.lua` file in `client/` | Which client files to send, paths from `client/`. |
| `[client] obfuscation` | `"light"` | How much to scramble client files: `"none"`, `"light"`, `"medium"` or `"strong"` ([Plugins on the server](/hosting/resources/#obfuscating-client-scripts)). |
| `[config]` | empty | The plugin's own settings, available as `node.config`. `node.resources.manifest().config` re-reads the file. |

The server refuses a path in `[server] main` or `[client] files` that leads outside the plugin's folder. If `resource.toml` can't be parsed, the server logs that and loads the plugin with the defaults.

## The Lua environment

The server half runs on Lua 5.4 with the standard libraries plus the global `node`, which holds the whole API ([reference](/plugins/api/lua/)). Each plugin has its own Lua state and can't see another plugin's globals.

On disk a plugin reaches only its own folder, so a plugin downloaded from someone else can't read `server.toml`, delete files or start programs on the host's machine:

| What | In a plugin |
|---|---|
| `io.open`, `io.lines`, `os.remove`, `os.rename`, `dofile`, `loadfile`, `require`, `package.searchpath` | Files inside the plugin's folder. A path counts from that folder; one from the server's folder (`resources/race/data.json`) or an absolute one also works if it leads inside. Outside the folder, `io.open`, `os.remove`, `os.rename` and `loadfile` return `nil, "…: outside the resource folder"`, and `io.lines` and `dofile` raise an error with that text. |
| `os.time`, `os.clock`, `os.date`, `os.difftime`, `io.write` | As usual. |
| `os.getenv` | `nil` for every variable: the environment holds the server's secrets. |
| `os.execute`, `io.popen`, `os.exit`, `os.setlocale`, `os.tmpname`, `io.tmpfile`, `io.read`, `io.input`, `io.output` | Raise an error that points to `[resources] trusted`. |
| `load` | Text only; precompiled chunks aren't loaded. |
| `debug` | Only `traceback` and `getinfo`. |

<!-- doctest: server -->
```lua
local _, err = pcall(os.execute, "echo hi")
node.log("%s", err)

-- expect: os\.execute is not available to resources
```

The same holds inside `node.job` and `node.await`. A plugin that needs more is listed by the host in `server.toml`; it then gets the whole standard library, with paths counting from the server's folder:

```toml
[resources]
trusted = ["backup"]
```

No plugin, not even a trusted one, can load a Lua module written in C. For what Lua can't do there are [native modules](/plugins/native-modules/).

## Several files

Relative paths in `package.path` count from the plugin's folder (the server's folder for a trusted plugin), and none of them points into `server/`. So `require("util")` finds `util.lua` in the plugin's root but not `server/util.lua`. Put `server/` at the front of `package.path` once, at the top of `main.lua`:

<!-- doctest: server {"files": {"server/util.lua": "local M = {}\nfunction M.add(a, b)\n    return a + b\nend\nreturn M\n"}} -->
```lua
local here = debug.getinfo(1, "S").source:sub(2):match("^(.*)[/\\]")
package.path = here .. "/?.lua;" .. package.path

local util = require("util")
node.log("2 + 3 = %d", util.add(2, 3))

-- expect: 2 \+ 3 = 5
```

`server/util.lua` is an ordinary module: it returns a table.

<!-- doctest: server -->
```lua
local M = {}

function M.add(a, b)
    return a + b
end

return M
```

## Reloading

`reload <name>` in the server console, or `node.resources.reload(name)` from code, replaces a running plugin without restarting the server:

1. The plugin's `resourceUnload` handlers run with the reason `"reload"`.
2. Its handlers, timers and coroutines are removed, and its Lua state with them.
3. The folder loads again and `main.lua` runs from the top.

`node.resources.reload` queues the reload and returns `true` if it was accepted. A plugin can reload itself.

`node.storage`, the files in the folder and all other plugins stay; whatever was in Lua variables is lost, so keep what matters in storage. Save it in a `resourceUnload` handler:

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local joins = node.storage.get("joins", 0)

local function countJoin()
    joins = joins + 1
end

node.on("playerJoined", countJoin)

local function saveJoins(reason)
    node.storage.set("joins", joins)
    node.log("joins so far: %d (%s)", joins, reason)
end

node.on("resourceUnload", saveJoins)

-- expect: joins so far: 1 \(shutdown\)
```

When the server stops, the same handler runs with the reason `"shutdown"`. Timers and coroutines started there never run, so save the data right away.

A reload doesn't send players new files from `client/`: the server packs them once, at start ([Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/#how-files-reach-the-game)).

## Errors and the log

An error at the top level of `main.lua` aborts the rest of that file, and the plugin stays loaded with whatever it subscribed to before the error. How these errors and errors in handlers look in the log: [API conventions](/plugins/conventions/#errors-in-handlers).

Log with `node.log`, and mark problems with `node.log.warn` and `node.log.error`; all three take `string.format` arguments.

---

# Events

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/plugins/events/

> The kinds of events, join and leave order, refusing a request with a reason, reserved slots, unsubscribing, and events that fire many times a second.

A plugin works in event handlers: `node.on(name, handler)` subscribes a function, and the server calls it when the event happens. Every event and its arguments are in the [events reference](/plugins/api/events/).

## Kinds of events

| Kind | Examples | What the handler gets | What to return |
|---|---|---|---|
| Server events | `playerJoined`, `vehicleSpawned`, `serverShutdown` | A `Player` or `Vehicle` object, if the event is about one | Doesn't matter. |
| Notifications | `vehicleEdited`, `vehicleReset`, `chatMessage` | The player, the car if any, and the data, JSON already parsed | Doesn't matter. |
| Requests | `playerConnectRequest`, `vehicleSpawnRequest`, `chatMessageRequest` | The player, the car if any, and the data, JSON already parsed | `false, "reason"` refuses. |
| Wire events | `greeter:hello`, any name of your own | The player and the data as a string | Doesn't matter. |

A name the server doesn't know is a wire event, a message from a client script ([Client scripts](/plugins/client-scripting/)). A client can't trigger a server event, and the server drops names that start with `node:`. Messages between plugins go over the [bus](/plugins/bus/), not through `node.on`.

Names follow these rules:

| What | Rule | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Server events and notifications | `<subject><Verb-ed>` | `playerJoined`, `vehicleSpawned` |
| Requests | `<subject><Action>Request` | `vehicleSpawnRequest`, `chatMessageRequest` |
| Wire events and bus messages | `<plugin>:<what>`, lowercase | `race:start`, `score:add` |

Several handlers, from one plugin or several, can subscribe to one event; they run one after another ([Timers and coroutines](/plugins/concurrency/)). Subscribing the same function to the same event again replaces the first subscription.

## Join order

Joining a server, a player goes through these events:

1. `playerConnectRequest`: the player has connected and asks to join. Bans are already checked, and you can refuse here.
2. `playerAuthenticated`: the player is admitted. The name and address are known; there are no cars yet.
3. `playerJoining`: the mods are downloaded, the map is sent and the game is loading the level.
4. `playerJoined`: the player is in the world. The usual place to greet, give a role and restore saved data.

Leaving is one event, `playerLeft`, with the reason the session ended.

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local function logConnectRequest(player, name)
    node.log("playerConnectRequest: %s", name)
end

node.on("playerConnectRequest", logConnectRequest)

local function logAuthenticated(player)
    node.log("playerAuthenticated: %s", player.name)
end

node.on("playerAuthenticated", logAuthenticated)

local function logJoining(player)
    node.log("playerJoining: %s", player.name)
end

node.on("playerJoining", logJoining)

local function logJoined(player)
    node.log("playerJoined: %s", player.name)
end

node.on("playerJoined", logJoined)

local function logLeft(player, reason)
    node.log("playerLeft: %s (%s)", player.name, reason)
end

node.on("playerLeft", logLeft)

-- expect: playerConnectRequest: Alice
-- expect: playerAuthenticated: Alice
-- expect: playerJoining: Alice
-- expect: playerJoined: Alice
-- expect: playerLeft: Alice
```

A dropped connection doesn't end the session at once. After `[network] lag_grace_sec` of silence the server fires `playerLagging`, and `playerRecovered` if the player comes back. `playerLeft` fires when:

- the player quits;
- the player is kicked;
- the player doesn't return within `[network] disconnect_sec`;
- the same account joins again while the old session waits on a dropped connection; the reason is then `Replaced`, and `playerLeft` comes before the new session's `playerAuthenticated`.

A player who reconnects in time doesn't go through the join events again.

Store a player's data under `player.accountId`, not `player.id` ([API conventions](/plugins/conventions/#which-ids-last)).

## Refusing a request

A request handler that returns `false` refuses, and the second value is the reason the player sees. The other handlers still run, and the player gets the first refusal's reason; only in chat does the first refusal end the chain. Returning nothing lets the request through.

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local function admitAccountsOnly(player, name)
    if player.guest then
        return false, "This server is for players with an account"
    end
    node.log("%s may join", name)
end

node.on("playerConnectRequest", admitAccountsOnly)

-- expect: Alice may join
```

The same works for cars. Here a plugin keeps one model off the server:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"spawn": "coupe"} -->
```lua
local banned = { pickup = true }

local function refuseBannedModels(player, requestedId, config)
    node.log("%s wants a %s", player.name, config.jbm)
    if banned[config.jbm] then
        return false, "This car isn't allowed here"
    end
end

node.on("vehicleSpawnRequest", refuseBannedModels)

-- expect: Alice wants a coupe
```

Changes to a car's parts or settings come to `vehicleEditRequest` as a batch of what changed, but `config` always holds the car's whole configuration after the edit. A refusal rolls back only that batch, to the config the server accepted last. The player sees the reason on screen; without one the car rolls back silently.

To watch a request without interfering, return nothing. Which requests exist and what a refusal does in the game: [events reference](/plugins/api/events/#cancellable-requests-decide).

## Reserved slots

On a full server `playerConnectRequest` still fires, with `player.overCapacity` set to `true`. A handler that explicitly returns `true` lets the player in beyond `max_players`, and a single `false` refuses whatever the others answer. If nobody returns `true`, the server refuses with `Server full!`, or puts the player in the [join queue](/hosting/join-queue/) if the queue takes them; `playerLeft` then fires with the reason `Queued`.

<!-- doctest: server -->
```lua
local reserved = { [42] = true }

local function admitReserved(player)
    if player.overCapacity and reserved[player.accountId] then
        return true
    end
end

node.on("playerConnectRequest", admitReserved)
```

## Notifications

Notifications report what has already happened. You can't refuse them, but they carry details:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"spawn": "coupe"} -->
```lua
local function logSpawned(vehicle)
    node.log("car %d spawned by %s", vehicle.id, vehicle.name)
end

node.on("vehicleSpawned", logSpawned)

local function logDeleted(vehicle, cause)
    node.log("car %d deleted (%s)", vehicle.id, cause)
end

node.on("vehicleDeleted", logDeleted)

-- expect: car \d+ spawned by Alice
```

Log the chat in `chatMessage`: by then the server has decided what became of each line ([Chat and commands](/plugins/chat/)).

## Unsubscribing

`node.off(name, handler)` removes one handler, `node.off(name)` all of this plugin's handlers for the event. A handler can remove itself:

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local function firstJoin(player)
    node.log("first player: %s", player.name)
    node.off("playerJoined", firstJoin)
end

node.on("playerJoined", firstJoin)

-- expect: first player: Alice
```

To run code after the other handlers have seen the event, use `node.defer(fn)` ([Timers and coroutines](/plugins/concurrency/#timers)).

## Events that fire many times a second

`vehiclePositionChanged`, `vehicleElectricsChanged` and similar events arrive with every packet of a car, up to 60 times a second per car. They pass only the car; read its current state with `vehicle:transform()` and similar methods. A handler that can't keep up sees fewer events, and no queue builds up. For a map or a radar, use a timer and one `node.vehicles.transforms()` call, which reads all cars at once ([Players and vehicles](/plugins/players-and-vehicles/#many-cars-at-once)).

---

# Players and vehicles

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/plugins/players-and-vehicles/

> Player and Vehicle objects, finding players, roles, kicks and bans, freezing, teleporting, spawning cars, tags, locks and scheduled changes.

Handlers get players and cars as `Player` and `Vehicle` objects. One costs almost nothing: a table with an `id`, whose other fields the server fills in on first access. Every field and method is in the [API reference](/plugins/api/lua/#player-objects).

## Players

### Finding players

| Call | What it returns |
|---|---|
| `node.players.all()` | Every connected player, by ascending id. |
| `node.players.get(id)` | The player with this id; for an unknown id, a player whose `isConnected()` is `false`. |
| `node.players.find(name)` | The player with this name, ignoring case; `nil` if there is none. |
| `node.players.count()` | How many players are connected. |

`tostring(player)` looks like `Player#3 Alice`. Two objects for the same player are equal (`==`).

### Who a player is

| Field | What it means |
|---|---|
| `name` | The in-game name. Still available in `playerLeft`. |
| `accountId` | The NodeMP account number; `nil` for a guest. |
| `verified` | `true` if the server checked the player's ticket with NodeMP. Always `false` on a server not in the list. |
| `guest` | `true` if there is no account: Test Drive, or a join with nothing verified. |
| `accountRoles` | The account's role in NodeMP itself, such as `"ADM"`; empty for everyone else. |
| `locale` | The game language, such as `"ru_RU"`, to answer in. |
| `role` | The role on this server, set by a plugin with `player:setRole`. |
| `ip` | The player's address as text. |
| `installId` | The launcher installation as NodeMP names it to this server: 64 hex digits, different on every server. `nil` if the launcher didn't report one or the player isn't verified. Hidden from other players. |
| `identifiers` | An array of strings like `nodemp:<id>`, `discord:<id>`, `ip:<address>`. Empty for an unverified player. |

Fields are read on first access and kept in the object. To see later changes, say in a timer or a coroutine, call `player:refresh()` or take a new object from `node.players.get(id)`.

### Roles

A role is a word the server keeps for the session and the game shows next to the name. Here accounts listed in `[config]` become admins:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"config": {"admins": [42]}} -->
```lua
local admins = {}
for _, id in ipairs(node.config.admins or {}) do
    admins[id] = true
end

local function assignRole(player)
    if admins[player.accountId] then
        player:setRole("admin")
        node.log("%s is an admin", player.name)
    end
end

node.on("playerJoined", assignRole)

-- expect: Alice is an admin
```

### Kicks and bans

- `player:kick(reason)` disconnects the player, who sees the reason.
- `player:ban(reason)` bans the account (if the player signed in), the launcher installation (if the launcher reported one) and the address, then kicks.
- `player:ban(reason, os.time() + 3600)` bans for an hour; the server lifts the ban itself.
- `node.bans.add(who, reason, untilUnix)` bans the address, account number or `installId` of someone not on the server; `node.bans.remove(who)` lifts a ban.

Bans are stored in `bans.json` and survive a restart ([Console, kicks and bans](/hosting/administration/#bans)). A moderator command built on these calls: [Chat and commands](/plugins/chat/#commands-for-moderators).

### Freezing and teleporting

`player:freeze(true)` holds the player in place: their cars stand still for everyone, and spawns, edits, resets and seat changes are refused with `You are frozen by the server`. `player:freeze(false)` releases them. A freeze lasts for the session; a player who rejoins isn't frozen.

`player:teleport({ pos = { x = 0, y = 0, z = 1 } })` moves the car the player drives, or the player on foot, and repairs nothing. If it can't, it returns `nil` and a reason: `"not_driver"` for a passenger (move the car instead), `"no_avatar"` when the player has neither a car nor a character on foot yet, `"bad_transform"` or `"unknown player"`.

### Separate worlds

`player:setGroup(n)` and `vehicle:setGroup(n)` put players and cars into numbered groups; group 0 is the shared world. Players in different groups don't see each other's cars, and `local` chat stays inside the group. Move a player's cars along with the player.

## Vehicles

`node.vehicles.all()` returns the cars without players on foot, `node.vehicles.all(true)` with them. `node.vehicles.get(id)` returns one car; `node.vehicles.count()` counts all, players on foot included.

### Who's who in a car

| Field | What it means |
|---|---|
| `name` | The owner's label: the spawning player's name, or the name the server created the car with. |
| `spawner` | Who spawned the car; `nil` if the server created it or that player has left. |
| `driver` | Who is at the wheel, or `nil`. |
| `authority` | Whose game simulates the car; usually the driver. |
| `passengers` | The passengers, as a list of players. |
| `isUnicycle` | `true` for a player on foot, whom the server also counts as a car. |
| `idleSeconds` | How many seconds nobody has driven the car. |

A leaving player's cars stay in the world without an owner until a plugin deletes them, as `vehicle-cleanup` from the [examples](/plugins/examples/) does.

### Tags and locks

Tags are short `key = value` notes the server keeps on a car and sends to every player: a key of up to 64 bytes, a value of up to 256, at most 32 keys per car; anything over is refused. This handler tags every new car, including the one the `/car` command below spawns:

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local function tagTeam(vehicle)
    vehicle:setTag("team", "red")
    node.log("car %d: team %s", vehicle.id, vehicle:tag("team"))
end

node.on("vehicleSpawned", tagTeam)

-- expect: car \d+: team red
```

`node.vehicles.byTag("team", "red")` finds every car with that tag.

`vehicle:lock("locked", { player })` lets only the listed players in, `"driver-only"` locks only the driver's seat, and `vehicle:unlock()` opens the car. The list can also hold `{ account = id }`, which survives a rejoin. A lock stops only new seatings and throws out nobody already inside. Until the plugin calls `vehicle:releaseLock()`, the owner's own setting doesn't change the lock.

### Spawning, moving, deleting

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `player:spawnVehicle(config, transform)` | Spawns a car for the player and seats them in it. |
| `node.vehicles.spawn(config)` | Spawns a car without an owner. |
| `vehicle:teleport(transform)` | Moves the car without repairing it. |
| `vehicle:reset(transform)` | Repairs the car in place or at a new position. |
| `vehicle:delete()` | Deletes the car for everyone. |
| `player:seat(vehicle, "passenger")` | Seats the player in the car, past any lock. |
| `player:unseat()` | Takes the player out of the car. |

The config is the table the game sends when a player spawns a car: `jbm` is the model, `vcf` the parts configuration. A position is `{ pos = { x, y, z }, rot = { x, y, z, w } }`, with `rot` optional.

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "/car"}]]} -->
```lua
local function spawnCar(player, msg)
    if msg.text ~= "/car" then return end
    local where = { pos = { x = 0, y = 0, z = 0.5 } }
    local car, err = player:spawnVehicle({ jbm = "pickup" }, where)
    if car then
        player:tell("Your car is number %d", car.id)
    else
        player:tell("No car: %s", err)
    end
    return { handled = true }
end

node.on("chatMessageRequest", spawnCar)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*Your car is number \d+
```

`cars_per_player` applies to `spawnVehicle` as to the player's own cars. The second value says why no car appeared (`"max_cars"`, `"bad_config"`, `"not_joined"`). `vehicleSpawnRequest` isn't called: the server doesn't ask itself for permission.

### Scheduled changes

To show another player's new car, or a change to its parts, tuning or model, the game builds the car and freezes meanwhile. So the client mod holds such changes back until the player is ready for them; what waits and when it is built is on [Settings](/players/settings/#other-players-new-cars-and-changes). `[vehicles]` in `server.toml` sets how a session starts ([Settings reference](/hosting/configuration/#vehicles)), and a plugin can change it while the server runs:

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `node.vehicles.setQueue("off")` | Every change is built at once, for everyone; `"allow"` gives the choice back to players. |
| `node.vehicles.setQueueMaxDelay(10)` | Every player builds what is waiting no later than 10 seconds after the first change; `0` removes the limit. |
| `node.vehicles.applyScheduled()` | Every player builds everything waiting, now. |
| `player:setVehicleQueue("off")` | The same for one player; `nil` hands the decision back to the server. |
| `player:applyScheduled()` | One player builds everything waiting, now. |

Before a race starts, every car must look the same in every game:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "/start"}]]} -->
```lua
local function startRace(player, msg)
    if msg.text ~= "/start" then return end
    node.vehicles.setQueue("off")
    node.vehicles.applyScheduled()
    node.chat.say("The race starts in 10 seconds")
    return { handled = true }
end

node.on("chatMessageRequest", startRace)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*The race starts in 10 seconds
```

The server itself forwards one car's edits at most once per `[vehicles] edit_interval_sec`, as the latest configuration. `applyScheduled` sends such held-back edits first, so they are built too.

### Many cars at once

`node.vehicles.transforms` reads all cars in one call, and only the fields you ask for:

<!-- doctest: server+client -->
```lua
local function countCars()
    local cars = node.vehicles.transforms({ "pos" })
    node.log("%d car(s) reported", #cars)
end

node.every(1000, countCars)

-- expect: \d+ car\(s\) reported
```

Each entry holds the car's `id` and the requested fields: `pos`, `rot`, `vel` and others from the [reference](/plugins/api/lua/#nodevehiclestransformsselect---arrayrecordidposrotvelangveltimepingseqpausedtransitioningteleportvelocitystephascontrolscontrolselectricsageseconds).

---

# Chat and commands

Source: https://docs.nodemp.com/plugins/chat/

> How the server's chat works, refusing and rewriting lines, logging chat, speaking as the server, a command router and kick and ban commands.

Chat is built into the server and works without plugins. Plugins are for refusing a line, rewriting it or taking it as a command.

## A line's way through the server

1. The mod sends a line with the scope `global` (everyone) or `local` (players in the sender's group, or everyone if groups aren't used).
2. The server strips control characters and cuts the line to `[chat] max_length`. If a player writes faster than `[chat] rate_per_sec` and `[chat] burst` allow, the server refuses the line and tells the player.
3. `chatMessageRequest` handlers pass the line, refuse it, rewrite it or take it as a command.
4. The server sends the line to everyone in its scope, the author included, and `chatMessage` tells plugins what became of it.

## The handler's answer

A `chatMessageRequest` handler gets the player and `msg = { text, scope }`, and what it returns decides what happens:

| Return | What happens |
|---|---|
| nothing | The line goes out unchanged. |
| `false, "reason"` | The line is refused; nobody receives it. |
| a string | This text goes out instead. |
| `{ text = ..., scope = ... }` | Replaces the text, the scope or both. A scope other than `"global"` or `"local"` refuses the line. |
| `{ handled = true }` | The plugin took the line as its command; nobody sees it. |

Handlers run in turn, each seeing the text as the previous one left it. The first refusal or `{ handled = true }` ends the chain.

To rewrite a line, return the new text; the server cleans and cuts it again:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "spam here"}]]} -->
```lua
local function maskSpam(player, msg)
    local clean = msg.text:gsub("[Ss]pam", "****")
    if clean ~= msg.text then
        return clean
    end
end

node.on("chatMessageRequest", maskSpam)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*\*\*\*\* here
```

To refuse, return `false` and a reason. The player doesn't see the reason: the mod shows a fixed line picked by its first word, in any letter case and followed by a colon, a space or the end of the reason.

| First word of the reason | What the mod shows |
|---|---|
| `muted` | *Not delivered: you are muted on this server.* |
| `filtered` | *Not delivered: the message did not pass the server filter.* |
| anything else | *Not delivered: the server blocked this message.* |

The server writes the reason to the console while `[chat] log` is on.

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "see https://example.com", "cid": 7}]]} -->
```lua
local function refuseLinks(player, msg)
    if msg.text:find("https?://") then
        return false, "filtered: links are not allowed"
    end
end

node.on("chatMessageRequest", refuseLinks)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:refused .*filtered
```

## Logging the chat

`chatMessage` arrives after the decision, with the outcome: `sent` is `true` if the line went out, otherwise `code` says why not (`"muted"`, `"filtered"`, `"blocked"`, `"handled"`, …). Lines refused before plugins (too frequent or unreadable) don't trigger it. Keep a chat log or forward chat to Discord here.

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "hello"}]]} -->
```lua
local function logChat(player, msg)
    if msg.sent then
        node.log("[%s] %s: %s", msg.scope, player.name, msg.text)
    else
        node.log("not sent (%s): %s", msg.code, msg.text)
    end
end

node.on("chatMessage", logChat)

-- expect: \[global\] Alice: hello
```

## Speaking as the server

| Call | Who gets the line |
|---|---|
| `player:tell(text, ...)` and `node.chat.tell(player, text, ...)` | One player, as a system line. |
| `node.chat.say(text, ...)` | Every player, as a system line. |

Both take `string.format` arguments. Color the text with `^` codes:

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `^0`–`^9`, `^a`–`^f` | A color. |
| `^#RRGGBB` | Any color. |
| `^l`, `^o`, `^n`, `^m` | Bold, italic, underline, strikethrough. |
| `^r` | Resets color and style. |

## Commands

The server knows no commands. A line starting with `/` stays an ordinary line until a plugin returns `{ handled = true }` for it: a command is a `chatMessageRequest` handler that recognizes its line. Several commands fit in a small router:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "/dice 20"}]]} -->
```lua
local commands = {}

function commands.dice(player, args)
    local sides = tonumber(args[1]) or 6
    node.chat.say("%s rolls %d", player.name, math.random(sides))
end

local function routeCommand(player, msg)
    local name, rest = msg.text:match("^/(%S+)%s*(.*)$")
    local command = name and commands[name:lower()]
    if not command then return end
    local args = {}
    for word in rest:gmatch("%S+") do
        args[#args + 1] = word
    end
    command(player, args)
    return { handled = true }
end

node.on("chatMessageRequest", routeCommand)

-- expect-client: Alice chat:msg .*Alice rolls \d+
```

The log masks the arguments of password commands (`/login`, `/register` and the rest of `[chat] masked_commands`) as `***`. The `chat-commands` example in the server archive adds `/help`, `/me` and `/pm` the same way ([The example plugins](/plugins/examples/)).

## Commands for moderators

The plugin decides who may use a command, usually by account numbers from `[config]`. Here `/kick` and `/ban` take a player's name and a reason, and a ban lasts a day:

<!-- doctest: server+client {"config": {"moderators": [42]}, "players": ["Alice", "Bob"], "emit": [["chat:send", {"text": "/kick Bob flooding"}]]} -->
```lua
local moderators = {}
for _, id in ipairs(node.config.moderators or {}) do
    moderators[id] = true
end

local function moderate(player, msg)
    local cmd, name, reason = msg.text:match("^/(%a+)%s+(%S+)%s*(.*)$")
    if cmd ~= "kick" and cmd ~= "ban" then return end
    if not moderators[player.accountId] then
        player:tell("Only moderators can do that")
        return { handled = true }
    end
```
